JSON: Name: v_atpase_extraorganelle_buffering Title: Genome-wide CRISPR knockout screening combined with targeted pharmacology and multi-omics to identify vacuolar H+-ATPase-mediated extra-organellar buffering that mitigates mitochondrial translation-induced dysfunction Short Hypothesis: Partial loss or pharmacological inhibition of vacuolar-type H+-ATPase activity increases mitochondrial membrane potential and improves cell fitness in cells experiencing impaired mitochondrial protein synthesis. Related Work: Prior approaches to identify cellular modifiers of mitochondrial dysfunction have used genome-scale CRISPR/Cas9 screens, small-molecule mitochondrial inhibitors, and pathway-focused genetic studies to reveal OXPHOS-essential genes, mitonuclear signaling (e.g., DELE1/OMA1 pathways), and mitoribosome quality-control factors. Complementary metabolomic and proteomic profiling has characterized metabolic rewiring during OXPHOS impairment and the integrated stress response. Separately, v-ATPase biology has been studied primarily for its roles in lysosomal acidification, nutrient sensing, and mTORC1 regulation; literature mostly documents complete v-ATPase inhibition leading to lysosomal dysfunction and cell toxicity. Limitations in existing work include: (i) screens focused on OXPHOS dependence without systematic induction of mitochondrial mistranslation stress; (ii) lack of integrated causal validation across genetic knockouts, pharmacological titration, and metabolic flux tracing; (iii) incomplete resolution of compartmental pH effects and their impact on ΔΨ; (iv) insufficient characterization of dose-dependent (partial versus complete) v-ATPase modulation and its differential cellular outcomes; and (v) limited cross-validation in primary patient-derived models. Abstract: Mitochondrial translation defects reduce membrane potential and impair cellular fitness in multiple diseases. We propose a systematic pipeline combining genome-wide CRISPR/Cas9 knockout screening under chemically induced mitochondrial mistranslation with targeted pharmacology and multi-omics to identify extra-organellar regulators of mitochondrial dysfunction. The approach uses parallel ACT-induced mistranslation and CAP-induced nontranslation conditions to distinguish suppressors of mistranslation-specific stress. Hits are validated genetically (e.g., ATP6AP1 knockout) and pharmacologically (low-dose v-ATPase inhibitors) and characterized by pH biosensors, TMRM ΔΨ measurements, untargeted metabolomics, 13C-glucose tracing, oxygen-consumption assays, proteomics, and ultrastructural imaging. The main contribution is to define a vacuolar H+-ATPase–dependent extra-organellar buffering mechanism whereby partial v-ATPase inhibition alters lysosomal/cytosolic pH and metabolic fluxes to restore ΔΨ and improve growth under impaired mitochondrial protein synthesis. Expected outcomes include a validated mechanistic map linking lysosomal pH, ΔΨ, and metabolic rerouting, with implications for targeting pH homeostasis in mitochondrial disease models. Experiments: Overview: Sequential pipeline with discovery (CRISPR screen) and validation (genetic, pharmacological, multi-omics, flux) stages. Replication: all experiments use ≥3 independent biological replicates; omics 4–6 replicates. 1) Discovery screen - Cells: HEK293 stably expressing Cas9. Library: Brunello pooled CRISPR knockout (~77,000 sgRNAs, ~4 sgRNA/gene). - Treatments: EtOH control; actinonin (ACT) 15 μM to induce mitochondrial mistranslation; chloramphenicol (CAP) 5 μg/mL to inhibit mitochondrial translation; ACT+CAP. Maintain coverage >500× sgRNA representation. - Readout: sgRNA abundance sequencing at day 0 and day 15. Analysis: MAGeCK/edgeR; gene-level Z-scores and differential enrichment (FDR < 0.05). Identify suppressors enriched in ACT vs ACT+CAP contrast. 2) Genetic validation - Generate CRISPR knockouts: ATP6AP1, ATP6V1A (or top v-ATPase subunits), MRPL44, C6ORF203, YME1L1 in HEK293 and U2OS (single-guide clones, verify by immunoblot). - Assays: 15 μM ACT +/- 5 μg/mL CAP; growth measured as cumulative population doublings over 15 days; viability by ATP assay. - Comparison: WT vs KO; statistical test two-way ANOVA. 3) Pharmacological titration - Drugs: concanamycin A (concA) and bafilomycin A1 (bafA). Dose-response range: 0.1 nM to 10 nM concA, 0.5 nM to 10 nM bafA. Identify sub-toxic concentrations (minimal growth impact over 72 h) and test with ACT co-treatment. - Metrics: population doublings, TMRM ΔΨ, OXPHOS complex abundance (BN-PAGE densitometry). - Ablation/Rescue: compare ACT-alone, ACT+low-dose concA, ACT+CAP. 4) Compartmental pH and ΔΨ - Sensors: FIRE-pHLy (mTFP1-LAMP1-mCherry) for lysosomal pH; BCECF-AM for cytosolic pH; TMRM (non-quenching, steady-state) for ΔΨ. - Conditions: WT, ATP6AP1 KO, WT+concA (selected low dose), treatments with ACT, CAP, FCCP (0.5–1 μM), valinomycin. Timepoints: 24, 72 h. - Metrics: lysosomal pH (ratiometric), cytosolic pH (ratiometric), TMRM fluorescence per cell (mean ± SD); statistical tests: ANOVA, post hoc contrasts. 5) Metabolomics and 13C flux - Untargeted metabolomics (flow-injection TOF MS) and targeted LC-MS for central carbon metabolites. 13C tracer: [1,2-13C2]-glucose incubation 60 min. - Samples: WT ± ACT, ATP6AP1 KO ± ACT, WT+low-dose concA ± ACT; n=6. - Outputs: total metabolite pools, isotopologue distributions for glycolysis, PPP, TCA intermediates; compute PPP:glycolysis labeling ratios, lactate m+1:m+3 ratios, fractional contribution to citrate (m+2, m+4). Statistical analysis by limma; FDR < 0.05. 6) Bioenergetics and proteomics - High-resolution respirometry (Oroboros O2k): basal, oligomycin leak, FCCP-uncoupled max, rotenone/antimycin residual respiration. - Label-free quantitative proteomics (DDA/DIA) of total and mitochondrial-enriched fractions; differential abundance analysis (limma, FDR < 0.05). - BN-PAGE for OXPHOS assembly state and immunoblot for OPA1 isoforms. 7) Ultrastructure and morphology - Transmission EM for cristae architecture quantification (cristae density, cristae junctions per μm2). Confocal imaging of TOM20 to compute fragmentation index (mitochondrial length distribution) using CellProfiler. 8) Primary cells and cross-validation - Primary patient-derived fibroblasts with mitochondrial translation defects (confirmed genotype). Treatments: ACT, low-dose concA; endpoints: ΔΨ (TMRM), growth over 3 days, metabolomics. - Baselines: healthy control fibroblasts; comparisons via two-way ANOVA. 9) Ablation/comparison studies - ATP6AP1 KO vs pharmacological partial inhibition (matched ΔΨ increase): compare metabolic rewiring and growth rescue to decouple genetic vs pharmacologic effects. - Effect of extracellular pH and glucose availability: assays in high glucose (25 mM), low glucose (1 g/L), galactose medium to force OXPHOS; compare growth and ΔΨ. Data analysis: CRISPR: MAGeCK/edgeR; proteomics/metabolomics: limma with empirical Bayes; multiple-testing correction Benjamini–Hochberg FDR < 0.05. All quantitative assays include effect sizes and 95% confidence intervals. Risk Factors and Limitations: Technical failure modes: off-target CRISPR edits or clone-specific compensations; antibiotic-induced pleiotropy (ACT, CAP) affecting non-mitochondrial targets; dye-based ΔΨ and pH probes confounded by probe accumulation, quenching, or altered probe kinetics under changed pH/ion conditions. Data and evaluation biases: cell-line specific responses (HEK293/U2OS) may not generalize to primary or in vivo tissues; patient fibroblast heterogeneity and limited sample numbers may bias conclusions. Scalability and compute: large-scale pooled screens and multi-omics require high sequencing depth and compute for differential analyses; batch effects in proteomics/metabolomics can obscure signals. Biological limits: partial v-ATPase inhibition windows are narrow—concentration-dependent switch from beneficial buffering to lysosomal failure; chronic inhibition may have systemic toxicity in vivo; metabolic rewiring observed in proliferative cultured cells may not translate to post-mitotic tissues. Causal ambiguity: correlations among lysosomal pH, cytosolic pH, ΔΨ, and metabolic flux may be interdependent, complicating attribution of primary causal mechanism from observational endpoints alone.
